w: Finished in 1997 at 328 metres, the second-tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere -- beaten only by Jakarta's Autograph Tower since 2022, after a quarter-century holding the title outright. It sits atop the SkyCity casino complex, and around 1,150 people a day still ride up for the view.
s: Auckland's skyline landmark, ex-Southern Hemisphere champ
_facts: Telecommunications and observation tower, 328 metres tall, completed in 1997
Was the tallest freestanding structure in the Southern Hemisphere from 1996 to 2022, now second after Jakarta's Autograph Tower
Part of the SkyCity Auckland casino complex; averages around 1,150 visitors a day

w: Opened in 1959 with four lanes of box-truss construction, then widened in the 1960s with cantilevered extensions bolted onto each side -- a patch job now carrying 170,000 vehicles a day. Walkers and cyclists have been promised a way across since 2016; two separate plans have been announced and neither built.
s: Auckland's harbour crossing, still promising a footpath
_facts: Eight-lane motorway bridge over Waitemata Harbour, original four lanes opened in 1959, widened with cantilevered extensions in 1968-69
Carries around 170,000 vehicles a day as of 2019, including over 1,000 buses
Two separate walking/cycling bridge proposals (SkyPath, Northern Pathway) have been announced since 2016 but not built

w: Its collections date to 1852, but the neoclassical building people visit went up between the 1920s and 1950s -- on Observatory Hill, itself the worn-down remains of a dormant volcano in the Auckland Domain. Part war memorial, part natural history hall, it has carried its Māori name, Tāmaki Paenga Hira, since 1996.
s: A war memorial museum built on a dead volcano
_facts: Collections and exhibits began in 1852; the current neoclassical building was constructed in the 1920s and 1950s
Stands on Observatory Hill, the remains of a dormant volcano, in the Auckland Domain
Known since 1996 by its Māori name, Tāmaki Paenga Hira; focuses on Auckland history, natural history and military history

w: Opened in 1922, and by 1956 it was staging chimpanzee tea parties -- imported straight from London Zoo as a global zoo fad of the era. Changing attitudes finally ended the act in 1963. What replaced it, decades on, is Te Wao Nui, a 2011 development built entirely around New Zealand's own native species.
s: The zoo that once ran chimpanzee tea parties
_facts: Opened in 1922
From 1956 to 1963 staged chimpanzee 'tea parties' with animals imported from London Zoo, part of a global zoo trend of the era
Opened Te Wao Nui in 2011, its largest development, dedicated to native New Zealand flora and fauna

w: Bishop Jean-Baptiste Pompallier, the first Catholic bishop in New Zealand, secured this land in 1841 -- rebuilt three times since, from wooden chapel in 1843 to stone church in 1848 to the cathedral finished in 1907. Auckland's Catholic diocese has called it home throughout, a Category I historic place since 1984.
s: New Zealand's first Catholic bishop's cathedral, rebuilt thrice
_facts: Land acquired in 1841 by Bishop Jean-Baptiste Pompallier, the first Catholic bishop in New Zealand
Rebuilt from a wooden chapel (1843) to a stone church (1848) to the current cathedral, completed in 1907
Mother church of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Auckland; a Category I historic place since 1984

w: Founded as the Auckland Yacht Club in 1871, granted royal patronage -- and its current name -- in 1902. Through Team New Zealand it held the America's Cup from 1995 to 2003, the first non-American club ever to successfully defend it, in 2000, then won it back in 2017 and defended it again in 2021.
s: A Westhaven yacht club that keeps winning the America's Cup
_facts: Founded in 1871 as the Auckland Yacht Club; renamed Royal New Zealand Yacht Squadron with royal patronage in 1902
Held the America's Cup from 1995 to 2003, the first non-American club to successfully defend it, in 2000
Regained the Cup with Team New Zealand's 2017 win and defended it again in 2021
Based at Westhaven Marina, facing the Waitemata Harbour and Hauraki Gulf

w: The mother church of the Anglican Diocese of Auckland and seat of its bishop, set in residential Parnell. The cathedral that stands today wasn't consecrated until 1973 -- a modern building carrying an old title, still the anchor of Anglican worship across the city.
s: Parnell's Anglican cathedral, seat of Auckland's bishop
_facts: Mother church of the Anglican Diocese of Auckland and seat of the Bishop of Auckland, in Parnell
The current main church building was consecrated in 1973

w: Known as Pukewiwi in one telling and Mount Roskill to most Aucklanders, this volcanic peak carries Tūpuna Maunga status -- an ancestral mountain, not just another cone on the city's long list of extinct volcanoes. The suburb around it borrowed its English name and kept it.
s: One of Auckland's ancestral volcanic peaks
_facts: Volcanic peak also known as Pukewīwī and Mount Roskill
A Tūpuna Maunga (ancestral mountain) in Auckland
Gave its English name to the surrounding suburb of Mount Roskill
